title: AI didn't cause the tech jobs bust, but it explains why there's no recovery
content:
Data analysis · Labour markets
Are tech workers cooked?What seven years of data say about AI and tech jobs
Tech employment in the United States has been falling for almost four years while the rest of the economy kept adding jobs. The easy explanation is AI. Seven years of data from the US, Europe, India and China tell a more precise story: interest rates started the decline, AI is why the recovery never came, and the cost is landing on the youngest workers in every market we can measure.
Every month the US Bureau of Labor Statistics counts the people on payrolls in what it calls the information sector. In September 2026 the count was 2,739,000. Outside the pandemic months of 2020, that is the lowest reading in more than a decade, and it is 12% below the peak of November 2022. Over the same four years the economy as a whole added about 4.8 million jobs.
It is tempting to draw a straight line from that peak to the launch of ChatGPT, which happened in the same month, and most commentary does. I wanted to know whether the data supports it. So I pulled every relevant series I could find: payroll employment and job openings from the BLS, Indeed's job-postings indices for six countries, CompTIA's analysis of tech occupations, the layoff trackers, India's labour survey and its largest job board, and China's official unemployment statistics. This article is what they show when you put them side by side.
The short version: AI did not cause the tech jobs bust. The timing rules it out. But AI is the best available explanation for why the bust is not ending the way busts usually end, and for who is paying for it. The hiring that has come back is for senior people with AI skills. The hiring that has not come back is for anyone trying to get a first or second job.
Timing
The boom died nine months before ChatGPT
The cleanest way to see what killed tech hiring is to look at demand before employment. Employers post jobs months before the hires show up in payroll counts, so postings move first.
Indeed's index of US software-development postings peaked in February 2022 at 2.3 times its pre-pandemic level. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in that cycle on 16 March 2022. By November 2022, the month ChatGPT launched, software postings had already fallen 36%. They kept falling for another two and a half years and bottomed in May 2025 at 63, more than a third below where they stood before the pandemic.
Employment followed with the usual lag. Information-sector payrolls peaked in November 2022, nine months after postings did, and IT services peaked in March 2023. The coincidence with ChatGPT is a coincidence of lag. The hiring pipeline had been shut off by rates in the spring; the payroll count simply took that long to turn.

2021 and 2022 were the boom. The information sector added 380,000 jobs in two years and IT services added 261,000, financed by near-zero rates and a pandemic surge in digital demand. 2023 and 2024 were the correction: 197,000 information jobs and 52,000 IT-services jobs gone, with announced tech layoffs peaking at roughly 262,000 in 2023. All of this happened while national unemployment sat between 3.4% and 4.2%, the lowest in half a century. Tech cut while everyone else hired, because tech had over-hired more than anyone else.
If AI had been the driver, the losses would track AI capability, which improved steadily from 2023 onward. Instead they tracked the cost of money. That is the first finding, and it is uncomfortable for both camps. The people who say AI destroyed tech jobs are pointing at a rates story. The people who say AI has had no effect need to explain the next three years.
The anomaly
A correction that refused to end
Corrections end. Once the excess hiring has been worked off, demand recovers, employers start posting again, and payrolls turn up. Every line of that script played out in 2025 and 2026 except the last one.
The Fed began cutting rates in September 2024. Across the whole economy, job openings returned to their pre-pandemic level: Indeed's all-jobs index stood at 104 in October 2026, and the BLS count of openings, 7.1 million, is roughly where it was in early 2020. Software-development postings bottomed in May 2025 and have risen 25% since. CompTIA counted 625,633 active tech postings in September 2026, the most in more than three years and 22% more than a year earlier.
And yet the information sector shed jobs faster in 2026 than in any year since the pandemic. It lost 103,000 jobs in the first nine months of this year, against 53,000 in all of 2025 and 68,000 in 2024. The pace, about 11,000 jobs a month, is slightly faster than in 2023, the year of the great tech layoffs. The year-on-year decline, 120,000 jobs or 4.2%, is the steepest since 2020.
That is the decoupling in one picture. Since January 2025, demand for software developers is up 16% and the number of people employed in the information sector is down 5%. Employers are posting more jobs and employing fewer people. In a normal recovery those two lines move together.
Two explanations are available. The first is macro. Inflation was back at 3.7% in September 2026 and the Fed had begun raising rates again, which squeezes the same rate-sensitive companies that cut in 2023. The second is that employers are hiring for different jobs than the ones they stopped filling, so headcount keeps shrinking even as postings rise. The macro story explains some of the weakness. It cannot explain why postings and payrolls point in opposite directions, or why the same divergence shows up in India, where US rates are beside the point. For that you have to look at what the new postings ask for.

In the United States, CompTIA's count of postings that ask for AI skills reached 349,821 in September 2026, up 282% since May 2024. That is 56% of all active tech postings. Indeed's economists looked at the rise in software-development postings between May 2025 and May 2026 and found that 37% of it came from roles with AI in the title or core requirements, and 71% from senior roles. Roles that require AI skills carry a wage premium of around 56%.
In India, Naukri's September report shows hiring for IT and software services down 4% on a year ago while AI and machine-learning roles are up 20%. Inside IT companies the split by experience is stark: AI/ML hiring rose 54% for people with 13 to 16 years of experience and did not rise at all for people with four to seven.

report.summary: Rate hikes, not AI, started the tech jobs decline; AI explains why hiring never recovered — and why the cost falls on junior workers.
report.background: Tech employment in the US information sector has been shrinking for nearly four years even as the broader economy added millions of jobs, and the convenient culprit is AI. The data tells a more sequenced story. When the Federal Reserve began raising rates in March 2022, the hiring pipeline had already been shut: Indeed's software-development postings peaked in February 2022 and had fallen 36% by November 2022, the month ChatGPT launched. Payrolls peaked nine months later, which is why the two events look connected. The 2023–24 correction — roughly 197,000 information-sector jobs and 262,000 announced layoffs at the peak — played out against national unemployment of 3.4–4.2%, meaning tech cut because it had over-hired, not because the wider labour market was weak. Since then rates have come down, postings have recovered, and employment has not, which is where AI enters the picture.
key_points: Timing rules out AI as the trigger. Software-development job postings peaked in February 2022, before the first Fed hike of that cycle in March, and had already dropped 36% by the time ChatGPT launched in November 2022. Payrolls peaked nine months later — a normal lag, not a cause.

The recovery broke the usual script. Since bottoming in May 2025, software postings are up 25% and active tech postings hit 625,633, yet the information sector lost 103,000 jobs in the first nine months of 2026 — its steepest decline since the pandemic.

Hiring demand and headcount have decoupled. Since January 2025, developer postings rose 16% while information-sector employment fell 5%. Employers are advertising different jobs than the ones they stopped filling, so postings rise while headcount keeps shrinking.

The new postings are AI and senior. 56% of active US tech postings ask for AI skills (up 282% since May 2024); 37% of the rise in software postings came from AI-titled roles and 71% from senior roles, with a ~56% wage premium for AI skills.

The pattern is global and hits juniors hardest. In India, IT-services hiring fell 4% year-on-year while AI/ML roles rose 20% — up 54% for 13–16 years of experience and flat for 4–7 years. China's AI postings grew roughly eightfold in seven months.
report.impact: The split between rising postings and falling headcount reframes the AI-jobs debate: AI is not a wrecking ball but a filter that reshapes who gets hired. Demand is concentrating in senior, AI-fluent roles, while entry-level and mid-level generalist work — the traditional training ground for new developers — thins out. That collapses the career ladder at the bottom, the stage where most engineers historically learned on the job. For the industry it means a smaller, more expensive, more specialised workforce and a widening wage gap between AI-literate and generalist engineers. For developers, the practical signal is that AI fluency now carries a substantial pay premium and that mid-career reskilling matters more than tenure. For users, expect software built by leaner teams, slower pipelines for niche products, and rising prices as labour-cost savings are not necessarily passed on.
report.tools: To track this yourself, follow the BLS information-sector series via FRED, Indeed Hiring Lab's postings indices, and CompTIA's monthly Tech Jobs Report (with Lightcast data) for AI-skill share; Layoffs.fyi tracks announced cuts, while Naukri JobSpeak and Maimai cover India and China. For skills, the Lightcast and Indeed wage-premium data point toward practical ML/LLM engineering coursework and open-source frameworks such as LangChain, Hugging Face Transformers and scikit-learn as reasonable starting points.
